newsitem.title: UK: Market holds breath for GEC shake-up annoucement.
newsitem.headline: Market holds breath for GEC shake-up annoucement.

text.p: Next Tuesday is make-or-break time for General Electric Co Plc as George Simpson, managing director, unwraps his long-awaited strategic blueprint to take the defence-electronics giant into the new century.
Results of the review are set to overshadow the annual results statement, with analysts predicting bold moves by Simpson who took over from veteran GEC chief Lord Weinstock last September.
The announcement will be given added spice by the shock departure of GEC's finance director David Newlands, who quit earlier this week.
The move was interpreted as a signal that Simpson is moving his own men into the top positions and finally stepping out of Weinstock's shadow.

Two key posts are now open and left to be filled by Simpson -- the post of chairman which is vacated by Lord Prior next March and now the post of finance director. Weinstock remains on in the honorary role of chairman emeritus since retiring.
Analysts welcomed the political manoeuvres, which boosted shares earlier this week, as a good sign for the review itself.

"We don't know what Simpson will announce. But one thing is clear -- it will be something dramatic, especially now that there has been a boardroom struggle and Simpson has won," said Andy Crispin, analyst at SocGen.
Another analyst added "The market is saying Simpson finally got rid of the old guard and purged the board. This clears the way for a possible deal with British Aerospace."

Rumours have re-emerged that the old adversaries are in merger talks once more, with Simpson's stronger hand adding currency to the speculation, said analysts. Simpson is understood to be keen to clinch a deal, as is BAe.

"The most optimistic hope for next week is that Simpson will announce news of talks," said one engineering analyst who added that it would make sense on the grounds that a merged group would be in a better position to negotiate deals and possible links with the already-dominant U.S. defence giants.
A merged group would be able to clinch better terms than they could as separate entities which would leave GEC or BAe as junior partners in any deal with the American giants, he said.
Other possible and less ground-breaking options next week could be a refocusing of GEC's businesses.
"We could see Simpson try to focus on one of the big three businesses, with defence the most likely," said Crispin.
"Some in the market would like to see the sale of rail or telecoms," he said adding that GEC might also announce plans to divest some of its smaller operations, with flat or low growth outlooks."
Its cash pile is estimated to be around 1.3 billion pounds ($2.2 billion) excluding joint venture stakes, leaving it huge scope for deal-making.
"The options for the cash are special dividends, share buybacks or acquisitions," said Crispin.
But one industry insider and former GEC employee said even if Simpson was radical, he would have a tough job on his hands after so many years of GEC drifting in a state of strategic slumber.
"It's like trying to wake up an elephant, get it to shift in a different direction and then persuade it to move in that direction. Not an easy job." he said.

SocGen's Crispin agreed "It's a fair description. GEC is like a dinosaur, let's face it. It's profits have been flat and it's seen low growth for years. Something significant has to be done to drive the shareprice ahead."

Looking at the results themselves, analysts are predicting year pretax profits of between 1.0 billion and 1.155 billion pounds, with a consensus forecast of 1.042 billion compared to 981 million pounds last year.
The total dividend payout is seen at between 13.1 pence and 13.8 pence per share versus 12.51 last year. ($ = 0.592 British Pounds)
